title: Heads-Up Poker Strategy for Canadian Players 2026
excerpt: Heads-up poker punishes weak fundamentals faster than any other format. Here is a practical strategy guide for Canadian players taking on one opponent.
author: Lisa Davids
bodyHtml:
Heads-up poker is the purest and most brutal version of the game. There is nowhere to hide, no waiting for premium hands, and no blaming the player to your left. Every hand you are either the small blind or the big blind, which means you are involved in every pot whether you like it or not. For Canadian players who have cut their teeth in six-max or full-ring games, moving to heads-up feels less like a new format and more like a different sport.

The good news is that heads-up poker rewards study more directly than almost any other format. The pool of decisions is small, the feedback loop is fast, and a player with sound fundamentals can beat opponents who are simply guessing. This guide covers the adjustments that matter most.

Why heads-up poker breaks normal instincts

In a full-ring game, a hand like king-seven offsuit is a fold from almost every position. Heads-up, it is a comfortable raise. That single example captures the entire adjustment: with only two players, hand values inflate dramatically because you only need to beat one random hand rather than eight.

Three structural facts drive everything:

  • You post a blind every hand. Folding your way to profit is impossible. Passive play bleeds chips automatically.
  • The button acts last on every postflop street. In heads-up, the small blind is the button, which reverses the usual blind dynamics and makes the small blind the aggressive, profitable seat.
  • Ranges are wide. Because both players enter pots with far more hands, top pair is a strong holding and second pair is often good enough to go several streets with.

Players who bring full-ring instincts to a heads-up table typically lose in one of two ways: they fold too much preflop and get blinded down, or they overvalue big pairs and pay off opponents who have connected with wide, unpredictable ranges.

Preflop: the button is where you make money

From the button (small blind), you should be raising a very high percentage of hands. Exactly how high depends on your opponent, but a wide, aggressive opening range is the default because you have position for the rest of the hand and your opponent must defend with weak holdings or surrender their blind.

The mirror image applies in the big blind. Because your opponent is raising wide, you cannot fold your way out. You need to defend a large portion of hands — calling with anything with playability, and three-betting a mix of strong hands and hands that flop well when called. The exact frequencies are less important than the principle: fold too much in the big blind and a competent opponent will simply raise every hand and print money.

Three-betting and four-betting

Heads-up three-bet wars escalate quickly. The key is to build a three-betting range that is not purely premium hands, because an observant opponent will fold to it every time. Mix in suited connectors and suited aces, which retain equity when called and can make strong hands that get paid.

Against opponents who three-bet constantly, the correction is not to tighten up. It is to four-bet more, including with hands you are prepared to fold if the pot escalates. Passive responses to aggression lose heads-up matches.

Postflop: aggression with a purpose

Because both ranges are wide, most flops miss both players. That fact is the engine of heads-up postflop strategy. The player who bets first on a dry board wins a disproportionate number of pots without a showdown.

But mindless aggression is not a strategy either. The players who win consistently think in terms of which board textures favour which range:

Boards that favour the raiser

High-card boards with an ace or king generally connect better with the preflop aggressor's range. These are strong spots to continuation bet, often at a small size, because your opponent has few strong hands and will fold frequently.

Boards that favour the caller

Low and connected boards — think seven-six-five with two of a suit — hit the big blind's calling range harder than the raiser's. Betting these automatically is a leak. Check more, control the pot size, and be prepared to give up when facing resistance.

Sizing tells your story

Heads-up players often fall into using one bet size for everything. A more effective approach uses small bets on boards where you can bet your entire range profitably, and larger bets on boards where you have a genuine range advantage with strong hands. Varying size according to board texture rather than hand strength makes you far harder to read.

Reading a single opponent

The enormous advantage of heads-up play is sample size. In a six-max game you might see an opponent play twenty hands an hour. Heads-up, you play every hand against the same person, so patterns emerge within a single session.

Watch for the simple, exploitable tendencies first:

  • Does your opponent fold their big blind too often? Raise every hand until they adjust.
  • Do they continuation bet every flop? Check-raise more and float wider in position.
  • Do they slow down on the turn after betting the flop? Their turn checks are weak — attack them.
  • Do they only three-bet with premium hands? Fold more against three-bets and steal relentlessly otherwise.

Exploitative adjustments beat theoretically balanced play against weaker opponents, and heads-up gives you the information to make them quickly. Bet-timing and sizing patterns are especially revealing online, a subject we cover in more depth in our guide to reading online poker opponents and table dynamics.

Bankroll and format selection

Heads-up has higher variance than most players expect. Because you play every hand, swings arrive faster, and a run of bad matchups can dent a bankroll quickly. A conservative approach is to hold a larger buy-in cushion than you would for cash games at the same stake, and to move down without ego when it shrinks.

Game selection matters more in heads-up than any other format. In a six-max game you can profit from two weak players even if the other three are strong. Heads-up, your entire expected value is determined by the one person sitting across from you. Refusing matches against clearly stronger opponents is not cowardice; it is the single largest edge available. Structured bankroll rules and stop-loss discipline are worth setting before you sit down.

A practical study plan

If you want to improve at heads-up specifically, the fastest route is narrow and repetitive. Pick a small number of spots — button opening ranges, big blind defence, flop continuation betting on dry boards — and work only on those until the decisions are automatic. Review your own played hands rather than watching highlight reels of other players; your leaks are yours alone.

Play sessions long enough to gather reads but short enough to stay sharp. Fatigue is a heads-up killer because there are no folded hands to rest during.

The takeaway

Heads-up poker rewards aggression, position and the willingness to play wide ranges without panicking. It punishes passivity ruthlessly. Start by fixing the two biggest leaks most players bring to the format — folding too much in the big blind and playing too tight on the button — and the rest of your game will have room to develop.
